title_en: Turning Back at Eight Thousand Feet
title_ru: Разворот на высоте восьми тысяч футов
description_ru: Горный гид и богатый клиент спорят на высотном лагере: идти к вершине или повернуть назад. Напряжённый диалог о гордости, погоде и мудрости вовремя остановиться.
text:
Karim: Mr. Ashworth, I know you are awake, because your boots have been moving about the tent for an hour like two nervous crabs. Come out and have some tea. The wind has dropped, but only to the level of a sulk.
Ashworth: I have not slept, Karim. I have been looking at the summit. It is there, in the dark, a perfect little triangle of ice, three thousand feet above this tent, and I have paid a small fortune to be in this exact spot. I would like to be told why we are not leaving at midnight.

Karim: Because the sky is lying to you. Look to the west, where the stars have gone soft at the edges. That is high cloud, a thin sheet of ice crystals, and it means moisture is coming. By noon, the weather will arrive like a very rude guest who has not been invited, and he will not leave until Thursday.
Ashworth: A few stars going soft? I have been sailing for thirty years, and I do not believe that a halo round a star is a reason to abandon a mountain. I have survived worse than a bit of cloud. I have survived a board meeting in Frankfurt.

Karim: I do not doubt your courage, and I do not doubt your boardroom. But the mountain is not a negotiation. Up there, above eight thousand feet in the thin air, your body runs at about three quarters of its sea-level strength, and your judgement runs at rather less. That is not a figure of speech. It is the strange, treacherous arithmetic of altitude.
Ashworth: You are saying that I am stupid.

Karim: I am saying that you are a clever man who, at this height, would make a stupid decision without noticing, and that the better you are, the less you would notice. I have seen strong, intelligent people stand on a ledge and fold their gloves with great care, while a storm was breaking behind them, because their brain had decided that the gloves were the urgent matter.
Ashworth: Gloves. How very undignified. I should like to think that I, at least, would be distracted by something noble, a glimpse of the infinite, perhaps, or a line of Wordsworth.

Karim: Nobody has ever been distracted by Wordsworth at eight thousand feet. They are distracted by their feet, their fingers, and their sandwiches. The infinite is a luxury for people with oxygen. Up here, one is philosophical only in retrospect, and usually in a warm room with a bowl of soup.
Ashworth: Then you are asking me to give up. After eleven months of training. After forty thousand pounds, and a wife who thinks I am having a very expensive breakdown. After telling the entire club that I would plant a flag on the roof of the world.

Karim: I am asking you to turn around. It is not the same thing, and I have been trying for fifteen years to explain the difference to people with excellent business sense. Giving up means you walk away and never return. Turning around means you accept that the summit is a place you may visit, but the descent is a place you must live. The mountain will still be here in the spring, and you may be, too.
Ashworth: That is a very pretty speech. Did you learn it from a postcard?

Karim: I learned it from a friend named Dawa, who ignored a high cloud on an October morning, and who is now a very fine rock formation that I pass every autumn. I say good morning to him. He has never been rude to me, which I regard as the only advantage of the arrangement.
Ashworth: I am sorry. That was a cheap thing to say.

Karim: It was a perfectly human thing to say. Every client says something cheap at this altitude, and most of them say it considerably louder. I have heard myself say worse. Now listen to me. We will wait until it is light. If the sky is clear, we shall climb as far as the shoulder, which is a beautiful place, with a view that will make your wife forgive the money. If the cloud thickens, we descend, and I will cook you the best dinner you have ever eaten in a tent.
Ashworth: And what if the cloud holds off? What if it drifts away to the east, and we find ourselves standing here at noon, in perfect sunshine, having wasted the only clear day of the season on a debate about stars?

Karim: Then I shall apologise, publicly, in front of the whole camp, and you may tell the story at dinner parties for the rest of your life. I will even supply a fitting adjective. "Timid" is the one most guides prefer. I would rather be timid and alive than bold in a photograph that somebody else has to carry down.
Ashworth: And the summit?

Karim: The summit is a rumour, a beautiful and slightly shifty rumour that has lured better men than either of us. The shoulder is a fact, and the dinner is a certainty. I advise you to take the certainties wherever you can find them. At eight thousand feet there are very few.
Ashworth: Very well. You win, you irritating, generous man. I shall wait for the daylight. Though I warn you, if the sky is clear, I shall be insufferable.

Karim: If the sky is clear, I will carry your pack, and you may be as insufferable as you like. Now drink your tea, and eat a biscuit, because your body is burning sugar like a furnace and your brain is the first thing it will rob. The tea has gone cold, which is how mountaineers know that the conversation was important.
Ashworth: One last thing. When the weather turns, as I suppose it will, I should like it noted that you were right, and I was proud, and that I did not enjoy either of those facts.

Karim: I will note it, Mr. Ashworth. I shall write it in the log in small letters, at the bottom of the page, under the weather and above the dinner.

questions.question: Why does Karim want to turn back?
questions.answer: High cloud signals approaching bad weather and altitude affects judgement.

questions.question: What does Ashworth say about his past?
questions.answer: He has sailed for thirty years and survived a board meeting.

questions.question: What happened to Karim's friend Dawa?
questions.answer: He ignored a high cloud and died on the mountain.

questions.question: What is the plan for the morning?
questions.answer: Wait for daylight and climb to the shoulder if the sky is clear.
